extracted.intended_audience: general public and practitioners concerned with bullying (educators, employers, health professionals, policymakers)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize definitions, contexts, prevention strategies, and recommended responses for bullying across settings (schools, workplace, professions, cyber). Intended to inform recognition, prevention planning, and intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workplace bullying (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Workplace bullying occurs when an employee experiences a persistent pattern of mistreatment from others in the workplace that causes harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactics can include verbal, nonverbal, psychological, and physical abuse and humiliation. Unlike school bullying, workplace bullies often operate within established rules and policies. Bullying is frequently perpetrated by someone in authority, though peers or subordinates can also be bullies. It may be covert or overt and can be missed by superiors or known by many throughout the organization. Negative effects extend beyond targets to employee morale and organisational culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trans bashing (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trans bashing is the act of victimizing a person physically, sexually, or verbally because they are transgender or transsexual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is committed because of the target's actual or perceived gender identity, not sexual orientation. (Noted distinction from gay bashing.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms/tactics of bullying
rubrics_metrics.description: Bullying can include verbal, nonverbal, psychological, physical abuse and humiliation and can be carried out to a person's face, behind their back or through the use of technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes cyberbullying; escalation patterns (e.g., blocking robots' paths then escalating to hitting and destroying them) illustrate how behaviour can intensify. Examples and studies referenced throughout article provide behavioural illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bullying in academia
rubrics_metrics.description: Bullying in academia is workplace bullying of scholars and staff in higher education and is believed to be common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Has not received as much research attention as bullying in other contexts. Can involve faculty, administrators, and group-level organisational processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bullying in blue-collar and male-dominated industries
rubrics_metrics.description: Bullying is prominent in blue-collar jobs (e.g., oil rigs, mechanic and machine shops) where intimidation and fear of retribution reduce incident reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In sectors dominated by males and where disclosure is seen as effeminate, underreporting can create a vicious circle. Manipulation and coercion of facts may be used to gain favour with higher-ranking administrators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bullying in information technology
rubrics_metrics.description: A culture of bullying is common in information technology, leading to high sickness rates, low morale, poor productivity, and high staff turnover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deadline-driven project work and stressed managers are cited as contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bullying in the legal profession
rubrics_metrics.description: Bullying in the legal profession is believed to be more common than in some other professions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The adversarial, hierarchical tradition contributes; women, trainees, recently qualified solicitors, ethnic minority lawyers and LGB lawyers are more affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bullying in medicine and nursing
rubrics_metrics.description: Bullying in the medical profession is common, particularly of student or trainee doctors and of nurses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conservative hierarchical structures and teaching methods may produce a bullying cycle. Relational aggression (gossiping, intimidation) is particularly relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bullying of anthropomorphic machines/robots
rubrics_metrics.description: Children have been observed bullying anthropomorphic robots: blocking movement, escalating to verbal abuse and physical destruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates that perceived human-likeness does not prevent abuse; provides an illustrative example of bullying patterns and escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bullying prevention (campaigns, laws, programs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bullying prevention is a collective effort including campaigns/events (Anti-Bullying Day/Week, International Day of Pink, STAND UP to Bullying Day, National Bullying Prevention Month), anti-bullying laws, and school-based programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-bullying laws in the U.S. have been enacted in 23 states making school bullying illegal. A 2019 study found school-based anti-bullying programs may lower incidence by ~25%. Prevention methods are often targeted at middle schoolers, where bullying is most prevalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness evidence for workplace interventions (Cochrane review)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Cochrane Collaboration systematic review found very low quality evidence to suggest that organizational and individual interventions may prevent bullying behaviours in the workplace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signals limited and low-quality evidence base for interventions in workplace settings—caution in assuming effectiveness; highlights need for higher-quality research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational programs and teacher training (Media Heroes example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs that educate teachers on bullying behaviours can help them educate and stop students from bullying; educating trusted adults about online behaviour can help prevent cyberbullying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'Media Heroes' program decreased bullying in participating schools. Emphasis on trusted adults becoming educated about online dynamics to reduce cyberbullying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responses: early recognition and intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: Addressing bullying behaviour early is important because it can be easier to control the earlier it is detected; attempts to ignore bullying often do nothing and allow it to worsen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early recognition is a recommended strategy; ignoring is an anti-pattern that can exacerbate the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responses: role of bystanders
rubrics_metrics.description: Bystanders play an important role: doing nothing can encourage bullying to continue, while small steps opposing the behaviour can reduce it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training bystanders (e.g., 'hero' training) and encouraging class-wide discussion can empower intervention. Research on bystander motivation and interventions is cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responses: role of authority figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Authority figures (parents, teachers, supervisors, HR, administrators) can be influential in recognising and stopping bullying behaviour and creating environments that do not encourage it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective actions include setting clear boundaries, communicating that bullying is unacceptable, and involving administrators. Many authority figures are untrained or unqualified and can inadvertently worsen situations, or even support bullies—training and appropriate response protocols are therefore crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective response principle: create non-permissive environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the most effective ways to respond are to recognise that harmful behaviour is taking place and to create an environment where it will not continue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes whole-class discussion of consequences, clear communication of unacceptability, and structural/support measures to prevent recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting prevention to developmental stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevention methods are targeted mainly for middle schoolers, where most bullying occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interventions and educational curricula should be age-appropriate and targeted to where incidence is highest; implies program design consideration for developmental stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting and detection challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Bullying may be covert and missed by superiors; intimidation and fear of retribution can suppress reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise cultural and gendered barriers to reporting (e.g., disclosure seen as effeminate in some male-dominated sectors). Systems should be designed to mitigate fear of reporting and to detect covert abuse.
